title: Tomas and the Sleepy Sunflower
markdown:
In a cozy town where clouds drifted like sleepy sheep lived Tomas, a boy with a curious mind. His best friend was Grandpa Lee, whose garden smelled of warm earth and happy flowers.

One sunny morning Ms. Meadowsweet brought a sunflower seedling to class. “We’ll watch it grow tall and strong.” Tomas promised to help: soft water, gentle songs, warm sunbeams. Even his spaniel, Sunny, rested a chin on the pot and watched the tiny sprout with kind eyes.

After a few weeks the sunflower seemed to pause. It stopped growing taller. Leaves looked tired. Tomas whispered, “Why isn’t it bigger? We’re trying our best.” Sunny nudged his hand with a wet nose.

Tomas visited Grandpa Lee with a small worry. Lee listened, slow calm smile. “Sometimes a plant needs its whole journey understood. Every plant has a story.” He showed his tall sunflowers. “Seed. Big plant. New seeds. That is its life cycle.”

Tomas looked closely. Bright yellow petals. Strong stalk. Nestled inside, tiny florets that would become seeds. Lee showed a dried head, full, ready to start again. “The classroom one might not have finished its story. It may need time to make its own seeds.”

“So it needs all the special steps?” Sunny gave a soft bark. Lee nodded. “Let’s map the journey.”

Together they drew: a tiny seed in dark soil; a sprout peeking, a leaf for the light; a stalk stretching, big green leaves; a yellow flower smiling, centre turning warm brown, hundreds of new seeds. Sun, water, rich soil. The seeds held the instructions.

Tomas took the map to school. “Not just growing tall. Seed, to flower, to new seeds.” Meadowsweet smiled. “The sunflower’s life cycle.”

They gave it more time and patient looking. Sunny napped near the pot, snores a quiet rhythm. The plant did not shoot up; it looked a little stronger. Tomas did not decide it had sighed or felt safe. He pinned the map beside the pot so the next pause would have a picture. Evening laid soft shadows. He, Sunny, and Lee walked home without promising dreams — only that they would check the florets again tomorrow.
